hooks.text: One giant arm dominates an entire spiral galaxy.
A single spiral arm stretches twice as far as its neighbors.
This spiral galaxy breaks every rule of cosmic symmetry.

title: The Galaxy with One Giant Arm
description: Deep in the constellation Aries, spiral galaxy NGC 772 defies cosmic symmetry. Its lopsided shape is the result of a violent gravitational tug-of-war.

beats.text: One giant arm dominates an entire spiral galaxy.
beats.visual: Hubble Space Telescope view of NGC 772 spiral galaxy, 2020

beats.text: Symmetrical spiral galaxies like our own Milky Way are balanced and orderly.
beats.visual: Illustration of a symmetrical spiral galaxy similar to the Milky Way

beats.text: In 1785, astronomer William Herschel discovered NGC 772 in the constellation Aries.
beats.visual: historical portrait of astronomer William Herschel, 18th century

beats.text: Instead of symmetry, this peculiar galaxy has a wildly lopsided and deformed shape.
beats.visual: Wide view of NGC 772 showing its asymmetrical spiral disk

beats.text: It features a single, dominant outer arm stretching far beyond the others.
beats.visual: Close-up of the long outer spiral arm of NGC 772

beats.text: This cosmic lopsidedness was whipped out by the gravity of a tiny dwarf companion galaxy, NGC 770.
beats.visual: View of the small dwarf galaxy NGC 770 near NGC 772

beats.text: This intense gravitational tugging ignited active star-forming regions inside that massive, stretched arm.
beats.visual: Artist concept of bright star-forming regions in a galaxy arm

beats.text: Cataloged as Arp 78, it shows gravity warping a cosmic giant.
beats.visual: Page from the Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies showing Arp 78

beats.text: That is why one giant arm dominates an entire spiral galaxy.
beats.visual: Full view of NGC 772 with its bright central nucleus and long arm

better_than_last: Addressed the reviewer feedback by highlighting the dwarf companion NGC 770's tidal influence as the definitive, high-impact cosmic payoff of the scale ladder.
